title: Empowering Financial Well-Being: A Comprehensive Approach to Managing Personal Finances of Employees of San Pablo Colleges Medical Center
tldr: A survey of 150 Filipino healthcare employees revealed strong budgeting awareness but critically weak saving habits and emergency fund practices, highlighting urgent need for targeted financial literacy interventions.
problem_and_motivation: Many individuals lack adequate financial literacy, leading to impulsive spending and insufficient savings. Filipino healthcare employees at SPCMC face particular challenges as wage increases fail to keep pace with rising cost of living.
approach: Collected data from 150 SPCMC employees using stratified random sampling.
Employed a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews.
Assessed awareness levels across four financial management domains: budgeting, saving, spending, and debt management.
Investigated personal, family, and social factors influencing financial management behaviors.
Evaluated practical application using weighted mean descriptive analysis.
Used weighted mean as the sole statistical treatment with a five-point descriptive interpretation scale.
findings: num: Overall awareness of financial management strategies is 3.21 (Somewhat Aware), with budgeting highest at 4.03 and saving lowest at 2.57.
num: Emergency fund awareness is critically low at 1.70 (Heard of it), the lowest score across all awareness indicators.
num: 65% of respondents do not engage in regular saving habits, saving only when surplus funds are available.
num: Saving strategies are applied rarely with an overall weighted mean of 2.33, the lowest application score.
num: 43% of respondents borrow money just to pay off existing debt (mean 4.34), indicating a debt cycle.
num: Social group belonging scored 4.76 (Always), the highest individual item across all tables.
num: Budgeting application is the strongest domain at 3.65 (Often), while saving is weakest at 2.33 (Rarely).
Overall application of financial management strategies scores 3.23 (Sometimes).

topics.name: Financial Structure of Filipino Young Professionals

topics.name: Financial Behavior of Filipino Young Professionals

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Provides an empirical baseline of personal finance management awareness and practices among Filipino healthcare employees, revealing significant gaps between budgeting knowledge and saving behavior. Documents the low prevalence of emergency fund practices and the prevalence of debt-cycle behaviors.
directly_justifies: 65% of Filipino healthcare employees do not engage in regular saving habits.
Emergency fund maintenance scores 1.23 (Never), indicating a critical gap.
43% of respondents borrow money to repay existing debt, suggesting widespread debt cycle participation.
Overall financial management strategy application scores 3.23 (Sometimes).
Social group belonging scores 4.76 (Always), the highest single measure.
limits: Single-site study limited to one medical center.
Uses only weighted mean analysis without inferential statistics.
Self-reported survey data may introduce social desirability bias.
Qualitative interview data mentioned in methods but not reported in results.

limitations: Single-site study limited to SPCMC, reducing generalizability.
Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference about financial behavior drivers.
Only weighted mean analysis is used; no inferential statistics or regression.
Self-reported survey responses may suffer from social desirability and recall biases.
Mixed-methods design claims interviews were conducted but findings not reported.
No comparison group or baseline period is established.
remember_this: 65% of Filipino healthcare employees save only reactively when surplus funds exist.
Emergency fund awareness scores 1.70 and application scores 1.23, the lowest across all measures.
Budgeting is the strongest domain at 4.03 awareness and 3.65 application, while saving is weakest.
43% borrow money to repay existing debt, indicating a widespread debt cycle pattern.
Social group belonging at 4.76 is the highest single measure, underscoring peer influence on financial decisions.
